title: Robotic magnetic navigation for atrial fibrillation ablation in older adults: is chronological age still the main concern?
Establishment and Assessment of a Predictive Model for Atrial Fibrillation Complications Following Off-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting - A Retrospective Case-Control Study.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF), the most common arrhythmia after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), occurs in 15 - 50% of cases.

OBJECTIVES: To investigate the incidence and risk factors of POAF after off-pump CABG (OPCABG) and to establish a nomogram prediction model.

METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled 179 patients who underwent OPCABG between October 2018 and October 2022. Patients were divided into POAF (n = 43) and non-POAF (n = 136) groups. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent risk factors. A nomogram was developed and evaluated for discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility.

RESULTS: POAF incidence after OPCABG was 24.04%, peaking on postoperative day two. Independent predictors identified were age, hypertension, left atrium anteroposterior dimension > 40 mm, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class ≥ III, and intraoperative potassium < 4.5 mmol/L. A nomogram incorporating these factors was developed. Validation showed excellent discriminative power (area under the curve = 0.919, 95% confidence interval: 0.8747 - 0.9637), good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.80), and significant clinical utility via decision curve analysis across a wide probability range (0.2% - 98%).

CONCLUSION: Age, hypertension, left atrium anteroposterior dimension > 40 mm, NYHA class ≥ III, and intraoperative potassium < 4.5 mmol/L were identified as independent risk factors for POAF after OPCABG, and these factors can serve as predictors for POAF. By implementing appropriate health management strategies, the POAF complications following OPCABG may be reduced.

title: Predictive Value of PET-Derived Myocardial Flow Reserve for New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) commonly coexists with coronary artery disease, heart failure, and coronary microvascular dysfunction, sharing common risk factors and pathophysiologic mechanisms. Whether myocardial flow reserve (MFR), a positron emission tomography-derived measure of epicardial and microvascular function, predicts incident AF remains uncertain.

METHODS: We included 10 500 patients without prior AF who underwent positron emission tomography MPI at 2 centers. The primary outcome was new-onset AF during follow-up. Multivariable Cox models adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, resting left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and LVEF reserve were used to evaluate the association between MFR and incident AF. Incremental predictive value was assessed using χ2, Akaike's information criterion, Bayesian information criterion, C-index, and a likelihood ratio test comparing models with and without MFR.

RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 640 days, 288 patients (2.74%) developed AF. Impaired MFR (<2) was associated with a higher incidence of AF (20.5 versus 8.3 per 1000 person years). In multivariable analysis, MFR was a significant predictor of AF (hazard ratio per 1 interquartile range increase, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.47-0.72]; P<0.0001), whereas stress and rest myocardial blood flow were not. MFR improved risk prediction beyond clinical variables and LVEF (C-index increased from 0.675-0.726 when added to clinical variables and from 0.758-0.770 when added to clinical variables, LVEF, and summed stress score; P<0.001). Similar incremental improvement was observed when MFR was added to the Cohorts for Heart and Aging Research in Genomic Epidemiology-Atrial Fibrillation risk score (C-index increased from 0.638 to 0.711). The association between MFR and incident AF was numerically greater in patients with preserved EF, although the interaction term was not statistically significant.

CONCLUSIONS: Impaired positron emission tomography-derived MFR is independently associated with increased risk of new-onset AF and enhances risk prediction beyond clinical factors and LVEF, suggesting a role for coronary microvascular dysfunction in early AF pathogenesis.

title: The Impact of Lifestyle Interventions and Mental Health Management on Arrhythmias in Heart Failure.
summary:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To summarise contemporary evidence on the impact of lifestyle interventions and mental health management on arrhythmias in patients with heart failure (HF), and to highlight emerging therapeutic opportunities.

RECENT FINDINGS: Lifestyle modification targets shared risk factors in both arrhythmias and HF. In atrial fibrillation (AF), weight loss, exercise, alcohol reduction, and risk factor management reduce arrhythmia burden and improve arrhythmia-related symptoms and quality of life. Similarly, in both HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), exercise training improves functional capacity and quality of life, whilst dietary interventions and weight loss are particularly beneficial in HFpEF. Mental health disorders represent novel targets for intervention for arrhythmias in HF; these conditions are common in arrhythmia and HF patients and associated with poorer outcomes, but early data suggests that mental health interventions do not reduce arrhythmia burden or cardiovascular outcomes despite improving overall psychological well-being and quality of life. Lifestyle intervention to improve physical health is central to HF and arrhythmia care and established as a central pillar of management. Mental health represents an important but under-recognised target which requires urgent further investigation.

title: Modified Posterior Wall Ablation in Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: the BOX-AF Randomized Clinical Trial.
summary:
AIMS: The efficacy of left atrial posterior wall isolation (PWI) for persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) is controversial. We propose a modified left atrial posterior wall ablation strategy.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of modified posterior wall ablation in patients with persistent AF who underwent first-time radiofrequency catheter ablation.

METHODS AND RESULTS: In this multicenter, single-blind randomized trial, 276 patients with persistent AF were assigned 1:1 to pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) with (BOX+) or without modified posterior wall ablation (BOX-). Seven participants withdrew, leaving 269 (BOX+, n=139; BOX-, n=130) for primary endpoint analysis. The primary endpoint was freedom from any documented atrial arrhythmia lasting > 30 seconds without antiarrhythmic drugs after a 3 -month blanking period. At 12-month follow-up, the primary endpoint occurred in 120 of 139 patients (86.3%) in the BOX+ group and 113 of 130 (86.9%) in the BOX- group (hazard ratio 1.046, 95% CI, 0.54 - 2.01; P = 0.894). The BOX+ group exhibited longer procedure time and ablation time. Acute successful PWI was achieved in 91 (65.5%) patients assigned to BOX+. In a nonprespecified, post-randomization analysis, arrhythmia-free survival was 93.4% in patients with acute successful PWI, 72.9% in those with attempted but unsuccessful PWI, and 86.9% in controls without attempted PWI (overall log-rank P=0.002). Adverse events were similar between groups.

CONCLUSION: Routine addition of modified posterior wall ablation did not improve overall outcomes of first-time ablation in persistent AF. However, achieving successful PWI was associated with significantly lower recurrence.

title: Novel cholesterol-high-density lipoprotein-glucose index is associated with 1-year recurrence of atrial fibrillation after catheter ablation.
summary:
OBJECTIVE: Insulin resistance (IR) plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of atrial fibrillation (AF). The novel cholesterol-high-density lipoprotein-glucose (CHG) index, which integrates total cholesterol (TC), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and fasting blood glucose (FBG), has not been validated for predicting AF recurrence following radiofrequency catheter ablation (RFCA). This study aimed to evaluate the association between the CHG index and 1-year AF recurrence after RFCA, and to compare its performance with the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 813 AF patients who underwent first-time RFCA was enrolled. The primary outcome was any atrial tachyarrhythmia lasting ≥ 30 s after a 3-month blanking period. Cox regression, ROC curve, net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) were used to assess predictive performance.

RESULTS: During 1-year follow-up, 142 patients (17.5%) had recurrent atrial tachyarrhythmia, with significantly higher CHG levels in the recurrence group (P < 0.001). Each unit increase in the CHG index was associated with a 4.23-fold higher risk of recurrence (HR = 4.231, 95% CI: 3.406-5.257, P < 0.001). The restricted cubic spline curve shows a dose-response relationship between CHG and AF recurrence. The CHG index yielded an AUC of 0.765, superior to TyG (AUC = 0.673). Adding the CHG index to the traditional risk model significantly improved NRI (0.434, P < 0.001) and IDI (0.200, P < 0.001), with greater improvement than adding the TyG index. Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent predictive effects across different populations.

CONCLUSIONS: The CHG index is an independent risk marker for 1-year recurrence after AF ablation and demonstrates superior discriminative ability compared to the TyG index.

title: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease, With and Without Increased Alcohol Intake, and Incident Atrial Fibrillation in Older Korean Adults: A Competing-Risk Cohort Study.
summary:
AIM: Older adults carry the largest burden of atrial fibrillation (AF) and a high competing risk of death, yet metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and MASLD with increased alcohol intake (MetALD) have rarely been examined separately in this population. We examined the associations of fatty liver index (FLI)-defined MASLD and MetALD with incident AF in adults aged ≥ 60 years, accounting for competing death.

METHODS: We analyzed 216 292 participants of the Korean National Health Insurance Service-Senior cohort screened in 2009-2010 without AF recorded before follow-up. Using FLI ≥ 30 as the phenotype threshold, participants were classified into FLI < 30 reference, MASLD, and MetALD phenotypes. Incident AF was ascertained from claims from 2011 to 2019. Cause-specific hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated with Cox regression and subdistribution HRs (SHRs) with Fine-Gray regression; MetALD was compared with MASLD using the ratio of adjusted estimates, and E-values were computed.

RESULTS: Over 1 833 772 person-years, 4292 AF events and 25 713 deaths without AF occurred. Compared with the reference phenotype, Model 2 HRs were 1.04 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.96-1.12) for MASLD and 1.27 (95% CI, 1.09-1.48) for MetALD; SHRs were 1.02 (95% CI, 0.95-1.10) and 1.26 (95% CI, 1.08-1.47). The MetALD estimate was 1.22 times (95% CI, 1.05-1.42) the MASLD estimate. E-values were 1.23 for MASLD and 1.85 for MetALD.

CONCLUSIONS: In older Korean adults, the MASLD-AF association was uncertain after adjustment, whereas the MetALD association persisted under both cause-specific and subdistribution hazard frameworks. The MASLD CI included the null, whereas the MetALD estimate was relatively more robust to unmeasured confounding.

title: Atrial Flutter in Adolescence Due to Invasive Cardiac Lipoma: A Rare Presentation.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Primary cardiac tumors are rare, with lipomas comprising ∼10% of benign cases. Although typically asymptomatic, invasive variants may infiltrate myocardium and generate significant arrhythmogenic substrate.

CASE SUMMARY: A 14-year-old previously healthy male patient presented with atrial flutter and was found to have a large, infiltrative lipomatous mass involving the right atrium, right ventricle, and tricuspid valve. Biopsy and partial debulking confirmed invasive cardiac lipoma, but complete excision was precluded by extensive myocardial infiltration. Despite antiarrhythmic therapy, he developed recurrent atrial flutter and ventricular dysfunction. Electrophysiology study identified a cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter that was successfully ablated; however, a second tumor-associated circuit was not amenable to ablation because of anatomical barriers. Sinus rhythm was restored with cardioversion and amiodarone with subsequent recovery of ventricular function.

DISCUSSION: Invasive cardiac lipomas present unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, often requiring multimodal imaging, multidisciplinary management, aggressive rhythm control, and consideration of cardiac transplantation in select patients.

title: Ablation With Dual-Energy Lattice-Tip Catheter for Refractory Ventricular Tachycardia Adjacent to VSD Closure Device.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Safety regarding pulsed field ablation (PFA) and radiofrequency ablation (RFA) using the Sphere-9 Catheter for ventricular tachycardia (VT) near ventricular septal defect (VSD) closure devices is unknown.

CASE SUMMARY: A 64-year-old man with extensive cardiac history including VSD closure with an Amplatzer device and complete heart block status post biventricular cardioverter-defibrillator with abandoned RV lead because of fracture presented with recurrent, symptomatic VT. Electroanatomical mapping showed VT in the basal septum adjacent to the Amplatzer device. Using the Sphere-9 catheter, RFA terminated the tachycardia, and PFA was successful near the VSD closure device without apparent complication. VT was noninducible postablation.

DISCUSSION: We describe procedural reasoning and considerations to optimize safe delivery of PFA and RFA using the Sphere-9 catheter for septal VT near intracardiac hardware.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGE: Colocalized PFA/RFA using the Sphere-9 catheter may be an effective treatment option for persistent VT near intracardiac devices for highly selected patients.

title: Comparative analysis of first-time pulmonary vein isolation in atrial fibrillation patients with heart failure with reduced versus non-reduced ejection fraction: A retrospective single-center study.
Task Force 8: Care of Competitive Athletes with Arrhythmias and Sudden Cardiac Arrest: Clinical Considerations and Electrocardiogram Interpretations.
summary: This document outlines recommendations for managing competitive athletes with arrhythmias and risks of sudden cardiac arrest, emphasizing individualized risk assessment, shared decision-making, and return-to-play protocols tailored to each athlete's cardiac profile and sport demands. It provides evaluation strategies for ventricular arrhythmias, implantable cardiac defibrillators, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern/syndrome, and syncope, alongside guidance for electrocardiogram interpretation in athletes. A key focus is placed on differentiating between low-risk and high-risk conditions, with recommendations for treatment strategies and ongoing monitoring to ensure athletes' safety.

title: Clinically suspected acute myocarditis with ST-segment elevation, multiorgan dysfunction, and reversible conduction disturbance in an older patient receiving maintenance hemodialysis: A case report.
summary:
RATIONALE: ST-segment elevation and marked myocardial injury require urgent exclusion of coronary occlusion. Maintenance hemodialysis adds metabolic, volume, biomarker, and bleeding-related uncertainty.

PATIENT CONCERNS: A 70-year-old woman receiving thrice-weekly hemodialysis developed chest tightness, dyspnea, and upper abdominal pain during dialysis. She returned with recurrent symptoms, severe metabolic acidosis, lactate 21 mmol/L, ST-segment elevation in leads V1-V3, and troponin I that increased from 13,019.45 to >25,000 ng/L.

DIAGNOSES: Coronary angiography showed unobstructed epicardial arteries with Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction grade 3 flow. Clinically suspected acute myocarditis remained the leading working diagnosis, but cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and endomyocardial biopsy were not performed and other causes of myocardial injury with non-obstructive coronary arteries could not be definitively excluded. The course was complicated by pulmonary congestion, metabolic and volume instability, hepatic injury, suspected pancreatic involvement, gastrointestinal bleeding, and symptomatic sinus arrest.

INTERVENTIONS: Antithrombotic therapy was reassessed after angiography and withheld when bleeding developed. Early continuous venovenous hemofiltration was performed without circuit anticoagulation, with heparin reintroduced later when clinically appropriate. Continuous renal replacement therapy was used for volume, electrolyte, and acid-base support. A temporary transvenous pacemaker was implanted for telemetry-confirmed sinus arrest with a maximum pause of 8.78 seconds.

OUTCOMES: The maximum R-R interval decreased to 1.97 seconds, permitting pacemaker removal. At approximately 3 months, syncope had not recurred, but persistent atrial fibrillation, New York Heart Association class III symptoms, and an left ventricular ejection fraction of 47% indicated incomplete cardiac recovery.

LESSONS: In a hemodialysis patient with a ST-elevation myocardial infarction-like presentation and non-obstructive coronary arteries, subsequent management should combine a structured myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries differential with explicit diagnostic uncertainty and repeated reassessment of bleeding, metabolic, volume, infectious, and rhythm-related risks.

title: Atrial fibrillation in chronic kidney disease - treatment standard.
summary: The prevalence of atrial fibrillation (AF) is high among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). While patients with CKD Stages G1 - G3b may be treated similarly to patients without CKD, little evidence guides therapeutic strategies for CKD G4 - G5 patients. Dosing of most drugs used for rate and rhythm control requires adjustment to kidney function. Recurrence rates after cardioversion and ablation for rhythm control are higher in patients with advanced CKD than those without it. Regarding the prevention of stroke and systemic embolism, the benefit-to-risk ratio of oral anticoagulation (OAC) is disputed among patients with CKD stages G4 - G5 with AF, in particular among those receiving hemodialysis given their high risk for severe bleeding events. Novel strategies for stroke and systemic embolism prevention, particularly factor XI inhibitors and left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO), have not yet fulfilled their initial promise as safe and effective alternatives.

title: Age-adjusted baseline D-dimer predicts thrombotic events during readmission in anticoagulated patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation
summary: Abstract Background Patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) remain at substantial risk of thrombotic and bleeding events despite oral anticoagulation, and readmission is a common and costly consequence. D-dimer reflects persistent coagulation and fibrinolysis activation and has been associated with adverse outcomes in atrial fibrillation, but whether a single baseline measurement can predict events during readmission remains unclear. Methods We retrospectively studied 1,108 anticoagulated patients with NVAF who had multiple hospitalisations at our institution between 2018 and 2022. Patients were stratified by baseline D-dimer according to an age-adjusted cut-off. The primary endpoint was a composite of thrombotic events, major bleeding and death during readmission, adjudicated by a hierarchical first-event rule. Multivariable Cox regression was performed in the 899 patients with complete CHA₂DS₂-VASc and HAS-BLED scores. Sensitivity analyses included propensity score matching (230 pairs) and a competing-risk model and a 30-day landmark analysis. The incremental value of the age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off beyond CHA₂DS₂-VASc was assessed by the C-statistic. Results The abnormal-D-dimer group had a higher incidence of the composite endpoint (24.0% vs 9.6%, P < 0.001) and of thrombotic events (19.7% vs 8.2%, P < 0.001). Abnormal D-dimer independently predicted the composite endpoint (adjusted HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.09–2.47) and thrombotic events (adjusted HR 2.02, 95% CI 1.30–3.15), but not major bleeding (HR 1.46, 95% CI 0.44–4.90) or death during readmission (HR 1.73, 95% CI 0.54–5.52). Sensitivity analyses were consistent for the composite and thrombotic endpoints, whereas bleeding and death events were too few for reliable estimates. Adding D-dimer to CHA₂DS₂-VASc improved discrimination (ΔC = 0.034, 95% CI 0.006–0.076) and reclassification (24-month NRI = 43.8%; IDI = 0.025). Conclusions In anticoagulated patients with NVAF, a baseline D-dimer above the age-adjusted cut-off independently predicts thrombotic events during subsequent readmission and provides incremental predictive information beyond CHA₂DS₂-VASc.

title: Sleep apnea is associated with new-onset atrial fibrillation in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis.
summary:
BACKGROUND: There are few data on the incidence and related risk factors and adverse outcomes of new-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) in patients receiving maintenance peritoneal dialysis (PD).

METHODS: In this observational retrospective, multicenter real-world study we included all patients that received PD for over 30 days in 2009-2019 in two research hospitals. The primary and secondary outcomes of the study were the incidence of NOAF and electrical direct current cardioversion (DCCV) during PD. Incident strokes and mortality were also recorded.

RESULTS: Altogether 401 patients with a median PD treatment duration of 1.6 years (IQR 0.9-2.8 years or 850 patient-years) comprised the total study cohort and 64 (16%) had a prior diagnosis of AF. NOAF was observed in 46 (13.6%) of the 337 patients without prior history of AF corresponding with the incidence rate of 6.3 per 100 patient-years. In a multivariable Cox model, cirrhosis (HR 5.536, CI95% 1.266-24.207, p = 0.023) coronary artery disease (CAD) (HR 2.268, CI95% 1.178-4.366, p = 0.014) and sleep apnea (HR 2.472, CI95% 1.010-6.048, p = 0.047) were independently associated with incident NOAF during PD but only the association with sleep apnea remained significant (HR 3.182, CI95% 1.399-7.238, p = 0.006) in a further multivariable Cox model adjusted with age, sex, CAD and PD vintage. Moreover, the observed percentage of NOAF during PD was as high as 50% in patients over 60 years old with a prior diagnosis of sleep apnea. Furthermore, 18 DCCVs in 6 patients and 27 (6.7%) strokes were observed and 100 (24.9%) patients died during PD care out of the total study cohort. The occurrence of NOAF was not associated with the incidence of stroke or mortality during PD.

CONCLUSIONS: In this real-world multicenter study, a substantially high incidence of NOAF and an expectedly low occurrence of DCCVs in patients receiving maintenance PD was observed. Furthermore, an independent association between sleep apnea and the risk of NOAF in this patient population was observed.

title: Effect of alpha-lipoic acid on atrial fibrillation and biomarkers of myocardial injury in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery: study protocol of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is associated with several postoperative complications, notably atrial fibrillation (AF), which may arise due to myocardial reperfusion following ischemia and the resulting inflammatory response. Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) is a potent antioxidant compound known for its ability to reduce oxidative stress and regenerate endogenous antioxidant defenses. The aim of this study is to investigate the effects of ALA supplementation on the incidence of AF and level of biomarkers of myocardial injury in patients undergoing CABG.

METHODS: In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-design clinical trial, 50 eligible patients scheduled for CABG will be randomly assigned into two groups to receive either 1200 mg/day ALA (ALA group, n = 25) or placebo (control group, n = 25), starting 10 days prior to surgery and continuing for 5 days after CABG. The occurrence of AF will be monitored using Holter monitoring during the first 72 h after surgery and electrocardiography (EKG) performed three times daily on postoperative days four and five. Changes in complete blood count (CBC), troponin I, creatine kinase-muscle brain (CK-MB), albumin, total protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) concentrations will be assessed at baseline, 24 hr and 5 days after surgery. The length of hospital and intensive care unit (ICU) stay will be recorded. Echocardiography will be performed at baseline and on postoperative day five. Dietary intake will be assessed throughout the study period.

DISCUSSION: This trial is expected to provide preliminary data on the effects of ALA supplementation in reducing post-CABG AF and myocardial injury. The findings may lay the groundwork for future research into the adjunctive use of ALA, alone or in combination with other antioxidants, to mitigate complications following CABG.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: The research protocol has been approved by the Bioethics Committee of Tehran University of Medical Sciences (No. IR.TUMS.THC.REC.1403.052) on November 10, 2024. The trial protocol has also been registered with the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT20131125015536N16) on November 14, 2024.

title: Painless Takotsubo Syndrome Triggered by Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): A Retrospective Observational Study of Seven Cases.
summary: Takotsubo syndrome (TS) as a manifestation of acute chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation is uncommonly reported. Emotional and adrenergic stress, hypoxemia, negative intrathoracic pressure, and the use of beta-agonists are frequently implicated in triggering myocardial dysfunction in this setting. We present a retrospective study of seven cases of TS in patients with COPD exacerbation in which none reported typical chest pain, representing a diagnostic challenge in patients with an apparent clinical justification for their dyspnea. All patients had electrocardiographic changes and elevated cardiac biomarkers, underwent echocardiography and coronary angiography or coronary computed tomography angiography, and received a confirmed diagnosis of TS. Five patients achieved complete recovery of ventricular function, one had partial recovery, and one died during hospitalization due to refractory ventricular arrhythmia. Systematic use of electrocardiography and cardiac biomarkers in COPD exacerbation enabled early diagnosis and appropriate management in the absence of typical angina.

title: Cardiac electro-structural remodelling and arrhythmia risks across the spectrum of obesity defined by the new Lancet framework.
summary:
AIMS: Obesity is linked to higher arrhythmia risk, yet BMI overlooks its complexity. Recently, the Lancet Commission has introduced a new obesity framework. We aimed to compare arrhythmia risks across distinct obesity categories.

METHODS AND RESULTS: Participants from the UK Biobank were stratified by obesity phenotypes. Co-primary outcomes included incident supraventricular, brady-, or ventricular arrhythmias, with secondary outcomes defined as their components. Obesity phenotypes were defined using five anthropometric measures, alongside ICD-10 codes, laboratory measurements, and self-reported data, to ascertain organ dysfunction. Of 487 806 included individuals, 36.6%, 18.7%, and 44.7% were identified with non-obesity, preclinical obesity, and clinical obesity, respectively. Compared to non-obesity without organ dysfunction, clinical obesity was associated with significantly increased risk for all primary and secondary outcomes (all FDR-corrected P < 0.05), as well as arrhythmia recurrence risk. Preclinical obesity was associated with significantly elevated risk of SVA and bradyarrhythmia, but not for VA or arrhythmia recurrence. Clinical obesity exhibited significant ECG alterations, including prolonged P-wave duration, PR interval, QTc interval, and QRS duration, accompanied by shortened PP interval, elevated ventricular rate, as well as altered P-wave, R-wave, and T-wave axis. For structural remodelling, clinical obesity was associated with enlarged left atrial volume and concentric left ventricular (LV) remodelling. A similar but less pronounced pattern of electrical and structural remodelling was observed for preclinical obesity. Compared to BMI, the Lancet classification's incremental prognostic value was small, mixed, and outcome-dependent.

CONCLUSION: These findings reveal a gradient of arrhythmic and remodelling risk across obesity stages, underscoring the need for early monitoring in preclinical obesity and targeted intervention in clinical obesity to prevent cardiovascular complications.

title: Case Report: Multimodal imaging diagnosis of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy complicated with thrombosis.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy (ACM) is an inherited cardiomyopathy, and concomitant intracardiac thrombosis is a relatively rare clinical complication, whose pathogenesis is linked to blood flow stasis, endothelial injury and impaired cardiac function. Timely and accurate diagnosis and standardized treatment of this complication remain critical to avoid embolic adverse events.

CASE SUMMARY: We present a case of a 37-year-old Asian female patient with ACM complicated with multiple thrombi at the right ventricular apex. She was hospitalized with a 3-month history of recurrent chest tightness and dyspnea aggravated in the latest half month. The electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with complete right bundle branch block, marked right axis deviation, ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in leads V1-V3, premature ventricular complexes, and prolonged QT interval, which may suggest elevated right ventricular pressure load; laboratory examinations suggested cardiac dysfunction. Transthoracic echocardiography detected right ventricular dilatation, diffuse apical trabeculation and mural thrombus. Cardiac magnetic resonance further verified abnormal right ventricular wall motion, non-enhanced intracardiac thrombus and late gadolinium enhancement supporting the diagnosis of ACM.

DISCUSSION: Transthoracic echocardiography enables early identification of cardiac structural lesions and thrombi, whereas cardiac magnetic resonance provides comprehensive evaluation of myocardial pathological changes. Combined application of the two imaging modalities is indispensable for confirming ACM with intracardiac thrombus. Early standardized anticoagulation combined with holistic therapy effectively lowers embolism risk and optimizes long-term prognosis. Clinicians ought to reinforce regular screening and targeted intervention for this rare thrombotic complication in ACM patients.

TAKE HOME MESSAGES: Transthoracic echocardiography serves as a convenient first-line screening tool for detecting right-ventricular morphological abnormalities and intracardiac thrombus. The mechanism of thrombus formation in biventricular-involved ACM with predominant right-ventricular lesions may be speculated with reference to Virchow's triad. Post-discharge imaging follow-up verified thrombus resolution after timely anticoagulation.

title: Case Report: Upper septal fascicular ventricular tachycardia mimicking supraventricular tachycardia: diagnostic pitfalls and mapping-guided ablation.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Upper septal fascicular ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a rare form of idiopathic left ventricular tachycardia arising from the proximal His-Purkinje system. Because near-synchronous ventricular activation can produce a relatively narrow QRS complex, this arrhythmia may closely mimic supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with aberrant conduction.

CASE PRESENTATION: A 25-year-old man without structural heart disease presented with recurrent palpitations for more than 4 years. ECG during tachycardia showed a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at approximately 200 beats/min with atypical right bundle-branch block-like morphology and marked right-axis deviation. Electrophysiological study initially raised suspicion for an AVNRT-like mechanism because programmed atrial stimulation demonstrated dual AV nodal physiology and intracardiac recordings showed an apparent near-simultaneous ventriculoatrial relationship. However, 6 mg intravenous adenosine did not terminate the tachycardia but unmasked atrioventricular dissociation, with the ventricular rate exceeding the atrial rate; together with subsequent Purkinje-system mapping, this supported a ventricular origin. Initial mapping identified an effective target in the distal left posterior fascicular region, where 30-W radiofrequency ablation terminated the tachycardia. The same night, incessant tachycardia recurred with a changed and narrower QRS morphology. Repeat mapping localized the final successful target to the upper septal region approximately 8 mm from the His bundle; 20-W radiofrequency ablation terminated the tachycardia without atrioventricular conduction injury. No symptomatic recurrence was reported during 12-month clinical follow-up.

CONCLUSION: A relatively narrow or progressively narrowing QRS complex does not exclude VT. In suspected SVT with atypical features, adenosine-unmasked atrioventricular dissociation should prompt reconsideration of a ventricular mechanism, while invasive electrophysiological assessment and repeat mapping may facilitate accurate diagnosis and safe ablation, particularly when the arrhythmogenic substrate is adjacent to the His bundle.

title: Cellular and molecular mechanisms of arrhythmogenesis in Takotsubo syndrome (Review).
summary: Takotsubo syndrome (TTS), an acute stress‑induced heart failure, is frequently complicated by arrhythmias that significantly worsen prognosis. Despite advances in understanding its pathology, the electrophysiological basis of these arrhythmias remains incompletely elucidated. The present review synthesizes current evidence to explore the core electrophysiological mechanisms underlying arrhythmogenesis in TTS, including abnormal calcium handling, repolarization abnormalities, altered conduction and refractoriness due to structural remodelling, and autonomic nervous system imbalance. The corresponding clinical manifestations of ventricular arrhythmias, atrial arrhythmias and bradyarrhythmias were further delineated, and contemporary diagnostic and therapeutic strategies were discussed. By integrating clinical observations with experimental findings, the present review aims to bridge the knowledge gap between mechanistic insights and clinical practice. Finally, critical research gaps were highlighted and future directions were proposed, emphasizing the need for personalized medicine and novel therapeutic targets to improve arrhythmia management and patient outcomes in TTS.

title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
summary: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

title: Task Force 6: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Competitive Athletes with Congenital Heart Disease.
summary: Athletes with congenital heart disease are commonly restricted from competitive sports participation based on limited data regarding exercise-induced sudden cardiac death risk. For most athletes, the myriad of benefits derived from participating in competitive sports outweighs the risk. This document reviews the cardiac assessment that may be considered for children, adolescents, and young adults with congenital heart disease. By utilizing anatomy, physiology, symptoms, and cardiac testing, together with shared decision-making, the authors propose a strategy to help guide medical providers advising their patients on sports participation.

title: Association Between Invasive Coronary Investigation Before Permanent Pacemaker Implantation and Mortality in a Historical Cohort with a One-Year Follow-Up: CorInPace Study.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: Permanent pacemaker (PPM) implantation is standard therapy for symptomatic bradyarrhythmias. In emergencies, limited assessment may lead to underdiagnosis of concomitant coronary artery disease (CAD).

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the impact of coronary cineangiography (CAG) before urgent PPM implantation on mortality.

METHODS: This cohort included patients undergoing urgent PPM implantation between July 2016 and June 2021, divided into those undergoing CAG (Group A) and those not undergoing CAG (Group B). The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality; secondary endpoints included mortality/readmission, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and hospital stay.

RESULTS: Of 895 patients, 841 were included (Group A: 160; Group B: 681). Group A patients were younger (70.2 vs. 75.2 years; P < 0.001), more frequently male (63.1% vs. 51.8%; P = 0.010), had more CAD (36.2% vs. 19%; P < 0.001), and less frequently had estimated glomerular filtration rate < 45 ml/min/1.73 m2 (10.2% vs. 22.9%; P < 0.001). Mortality (hazard ratio [HR] 0.96, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.56 - 1.66; P = 0.898) and mortality/readmission (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.74 - 1.50; P = 0.776) did not differ between groups. Multivariate analysis showed no significant impact of CAG on either outcome. ACS was more frequent in Group A (7.5% vs. 2.7%; P = 0.005), and hospital stay was shorter in Group B (6 vs. 9 days; P < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: In our study, CAG before PPM implantation was not associated with mortality or mortality/readmission but was associated with longer hospitalization and a higher incidence of ACS.

title: Left Bundle Branch Optimized Resynchronization Therapy for Persistent Ventricular Dysfunction After Complex PCI and TAVR.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Severe aortic stenosis with complex coronary artery disease presents challenges in patients unsuitable for surgery. Persistent left bundle branch block (LBBB) after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) may impair ventricular recovery.

CASE SUMMARY: A 67-year-old man underwent high-risk left main-left anterior descending percutaneous coronary intervention, complicated by cardiogenic shock and severe left ventricular (LV) dysfunction. Subsequent TAVR achieved favorable valve hemodynamics but was followed by new-onset left bundle branch block and persistent LV dysfunction. Left bundle branch pacing achieved complete correction only at high output. A coronary sinus lead was added for left bundle branch-optimized cardiac resynchronization therapy with a defibrillator (LOT-CRTD). At 3 months, LV function fully recovered with reverse remodeling and marked symptom improvement. Why Beyond the Guideline: Optimal percutaneous coronary intervention-TAVR timing and device strategies for post-TAVR LBBB with LV dysfunction remain poorly defined in current guidelines.

DISCUSSION: LOT-CRTD may provide effective cardiac resynchronization when isolated left bundle branch pacing cannot achieve optimal correction.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGE: Sequence of PCI-TAVR remained individualized. LOT-CRT is a viable strategy to facilitate ventricular recovery for post-TAVR LBBB.

title: Safety and Efficacy of Transvenous Lead Extraction Using a Right-Sided Approach.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Despite extensive experience with transvenous lead extraction (TLE) overall, outcomes for systems implanted on the right chest remain underexplored, largely because of their low incidence.

OBJECTIVES: The objective was to evaluate whether system laterality influences TLE outcomes.

METHODS: Using our institutional, prospectively maintained ExTRACT registry, we analyzed all consecutive patients undergoing TLE procedures at the Cleveland Clinic between 1996 and 2022. Patients were categorized by system laterality. Baseline characteristics, procedural characteristics, and complications were assessed. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated the association between right-sided TLE and adverse events.

RESULTS: Among 4,989 patients, 494 (9.9%) had right-sided and 4,495 (90.1%) had left-sided TLE. Compared with left-sided cases, right-sided cases had longer total lead dwell times (13.83 vs 9.26 years, P < 0.001) and were more likely to be extracted because of infection (47.57% vs 39.71%, P = 0.001). Fluoroscopy time was longer (15.95 vs 12.1 minutes; P < 0.001), and femoral workstation use more frequent (7.89% vs 4.05%, P < 0.001), yet complete extraction was lower (94.53% vs 96.44%, P = 0.034). Right-sided TLE had higher rates of sternotomy (2.83% vs 1.25%, P = 0.004) and superior vena cava or right atrial tear/perforation (2.49% vs 1.10%, P = 0.009). Thirty-day mortality was low and comparable (0.61% vs 0.47%, P = 0.727). Multivariable regression showed that right-sided TLE was associated with higher odds of sternotomy (OR = 1.92, 95% CI: 1.01-3.46, P = 0.037) and superior vena cava or right atrial tear/perforation (OR = 2.02, 95% CI: 1.01-3.78, P = 0.037).

CONCLUSIONS: Right-sided TLE is associated with a lower rate of complete extraction and increased procedural risk, particularly sternotomy and major vascular injury, compared with left-sided TLE. These findings should be carefully weighed when implanting or extracting right-sided systems.

title: Cardiovascular events and interventions in patients with light chain amyloidosis: a real-world study in the United States.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Light chain amyloidosis (AL amyloidosis) is a rare disease characterized by the deposition of misfolded immunoglobulin light chains, often in the heart, and is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular (CV) events. We evaluated the incidence of CV events and interventions among US patients with AL amyloidosis.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted using data from the Optum® de-identified Electronic Health Record (EHR) dataset (~ 106 million patients). Adults with AL amyloidosis were identified by ≥ 2 ICD-10-CM codes (E85.81) or positive mentions in the physician notes (≥ 30 days apart). Patients with ≥ 12 months of pre-index clinical data (index = first diagnosis between January 01, 2017 - March 31, 2021) were included. Cases with transthyretin amyloidosis were excluded unless AL-specific treatment was not evident. CV events (e.g. heart failure) and interventions (e.g. pacemaker) were captured from index to death or study end (March 31, 2022). Incidence and patient‑level event rates were calculated by overall and by stage of cardiac involvement(the European modification of 2004 Mayo staging systems were used for this purpose).

RESULTS: A total of 1,859 patients (mean age 66.9 years, 53.9% male) were included in the study. Over a mean follow-up duration of 2.1 years, 64.6% of patients experienced at least one coded CV diagnosis and 16.7% underwent at least one CV intervention during follow-up. Incidence rates (IR) per 100,000 person-years (PY) were 22,068 for CV events and 6,278 for CV interventions. Patient‑level event rates were 61,801 per 100,000 PY for CV events and 8,962 per 100,000 PY, for CV interventions, respectively. Common coded CV diagnoses included conduction disorder and arrhythmias (28,334), heart failure (23,869), and cardiomyopathy (18,833). Most frequent interventions were pacemaker implantation (2,867), cardiac defibrillator implantation (2,349), and angioplasty/bypass (739). The incidence of heart transplant was 228 events per 100,000 PY. The cumulative incidence of CV events increased with disease stage: 38.3% (stage I), 70.3% (II), 81.8% (IIIa), and 89.6% (IIIb) at 30 months (all p < 0.001 vs stage I). The CV intervention cumulative incidence in stage IIIa reached 31.3% at 36 months. Similar findings were observed for stage IIIb.

CONCLUSIONS: Despite therapeutic advances, patients with AL amyloidosis experience a substantial burden of coded CV diagnoses and interventions in real‑world clinical practice, particularly among those with advanced disease stage. Increased clinician recognition of this rare disease, enabling earlier diagnosis and timely initiation of appropriate therapy, together with an improved understanding of CV progression, is essential to guide management and reduce morbidity.

title: Molecular to Clinical Perspectives in Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy: Current Understanding and Future Therapeutic Directions.
summary: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM), a genetic heart muscle disease that affects primarily the right ventricle, can lead to sudden cardiac death. Although ACM was initially classified as a dysplasia due to a congenital abnormality in the growth of the right ventricle, it was later demonstrated to be caused by a genetic defect in the cardiac desmosomes. Mutations in genes that encode components of the desmosomes, that is, the adhesive junctions that connect cardiomyocytes, are the most common cause of ACMs. However, the specific molecular mechanisms that lead to myocardial destruction, remodeling, and arrhythmogenic predisposition are unclear. Recent advances in the understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms of ACM have focused on mechanisms including cardiomyocyte loss, fibrosis, and adipogenesis, which occur through different signaling pathways such as Wnt signaling, PPARγ signaling, and the Hippo-Yes-associated protein pathway. Inflammation also plays a role in the development of ACM. Regarding the diagnosis of ACM, the International Task Force Criteria distinguish between minor and major ACM criteria, with an emphasis on family history, conduction defects, morphological and microstructural changes, repolarization defects, and arrhythmias. In the management and prevention of sudden cardiac death and ventricular tachyarrhythmias, epicardial and endocardial ablation with electromagnetic mapping and the use of an implantable cardiac defibrillator have emerged as useful approaches. We provide an overview of the genetics, histological features, molecular mechanisms, clinical presentation, diagnosis, biomarkers and treatment advances of ACM, including gene therapy, small-molecule and drug-based therapies, implantable cardioverter defibrillators, radiofrequency ablation, lifestyle interventions, heart transplantation and prognosis.

title: Hypokalaemia-Induced Arrhythmias: Mechanisms of hERG Channel Dysregulation and Current Therapeutic Strategies
summary: Hypokalaemia is an independent risk factor for sudden cardiac death, affecting 7–17% of cardiovascular patients. This review examines mechanisms of hypokalaemia-induced arrhythmias, focusing on the human ether-a-go-go-related gene (hERG) potassium channel. Low extracellular potassium inhibits the Na+/K+ -ATPase and suppresses repolarising potassium currents, converging on intracellular calcium overload and action potential prolongation. These changes trigger calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) activation, which phosphorylates ion channels to amplify arrhythmia substrate through early and delayed afterdepolarisations and re-entry. Critically, hERG undergoes chronic internalisation and degradation in hypokalaemia, functioning as an acquired channelopathy. Current management is reactive and relies on potassium supplementation, which incompletely addresses these molecular remodelling processes. Emerging pharmacological strategies targeting RyR2, CaMKII, and the late sodium current show promise, but mechanistic insights suggest that multi-mechanistic strategies which also maintain hERG may offer superior protection, particularly in structurally remodelled hearts. Understanding these mechanisms identifies therapeutic targets beyond electrolyte replacement.
journal: International Journal of Drug Discovery and Pharmacology
